meta.title: Who really said "Those who deny freedom to others deserve it not for themselves, and, under a just God, cannot long retain it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — genuinely Abraham Lincoln, from his 6 April 1859 letter to Henry L. Pierce and others. A rare case where the famous name is the real source.

meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Abraham Lincoln, from his 6 April 1859 letter to Henry L. Pierce & others on Jefferson. Confirmed against the Collected Works.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Lincoln really wrote this. It closes his letter of 6 April 1859 to Henry L. Pierce and others, declining an invitation to a Boston festival honoring Thomas Jefferson’s birthday. His manuscript reads with slightly heavier punctuation — “Those who deny freedom to others, deserve it not for themselves; and, under a just God, can not long retain it” — and the widely circulated form merely modernizes the commas and spelling.

source.excerpt: This is a world of compensations; and he who would be no slave, must consent to have no slave. Those who deny freedom to others, deserve it not for themselves; and, under a just God, can not long retain it.
trail: Lincoln’s full letter, with this closing sentence, is reproduced at Abraham Lincoln Online.
The Smithsonian American Art Museum holds Fred Conway’s 1953 painting bearing the exact quotation, attributed to the 6 April 1859 letter to H. L. Pierce.
The letter is catalogued and transcribed by Teaching American History as an 1859 Lincoln document.

author.name: Abraham Lincoln
author.heading: About Abraham Lincoln
author.bio: Abraham Lincoln led the United States through the Civil War and issued the Emancipation Proclamation. A largely self-taught lawyer from Illinois, he built his political identity around the antislavery reading of the Declaration of Independence. This line comes from an 1859 letter defending Jefferson’s principle that liberty is a universal, reciprocal claim — a theme that runs through his speeches from Peoria to Gettysburg.

misattribution.heading: A genuine one — with a caveat
misattribution.intro: Unusually for a quote pinned to a famous name, this really is Lincoln. The only distortion is cosmetic: the version everyone shares has been lightly repunctuated and modernized from what Lincoln actually wrote.

items.why: Lincoln’s manuscript reads “Those who deny freedom to others, deserve it not for themselves; and, under a just God, can not long retain it” — two extra commas, a semicolon, and the older “can not.” The popular form smooths these into “cannot,” per the original letter.

items.who: Not a speech or the Emancipation era
items.why: It is sometimes floated as if from a great oration; in fact it closes a short 1859 letter declining a Jefferson-birthday dinner in Boston, written two years before Lincoln became president, as documented by Teaching American History.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought and the words are Lincoln’s own, from his 6 April 1859 letter to Henry L. Pierce and others — only the punctuation has drifted.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Lincoln wrote to a committee of Boston Republicans who had invited him to a festival marking Thomas Jefferson’s birthday. Unable to attend, he used the letter to reclaim Jefferson — and the Declaration’s “all men are created equal” — from those who, he argued, had reduced liberty to a matter of party and property.

The line distills his core argument: freedom is reciprocal. A nation that denies liberty to some forfeits its own claim to it, “under a just God.” The same reasoning would resurface in the House Divided speech and, ultimately, the wartime case against slavery.
